strengths: Well-motivated architecture: DUST successfully addresses the modality conflict between low-dimensional, temporally smooth action trajectories and high-dimensional, spatially structured future visual observations by maintaining separate streams with shared cross-modal attention.

Solid theoretical and methodological contributions: The decoupled flow-matching training framework allows the model to learn bidirectional relationships (forward and inverse dynamics) in a principled way. The asynchronous joint sampling provides a neat way to scale up performance at test-time.

Comprehensive and high-quality experiments: The method is validated on both simulated (RoboCasa, GR-1) and real-world benchmarks (Franka), showing consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines like GR00T-N1.5.

Transfer learning potential: Successfully leveraging action-free videos (BridgeV2) for world-model pre-training demonstrates the scalability and usefulness of the approach for data-efficient robot learning.

Excellent reproducibility details: The authors provide detailed ablation studies, hyperparameter choices, and pseudocode for both the decoupled training and asynchronous joint sampling in the appendix.
weaknesses: Lack of detailed inference speed/latency analysis: While test-time scaling (increasing $N_o$) is shown to improve success rates, running more denoising steps over the joint MMDiT backbone will inevitably increase inference latency. The paper would benefit from a quantitative analysis of this trade-off (e.g., success rate vs. inference latency/FPS).

Reimplementation of baselines: The FLARE baseline is a custom reimplementation due to the lack of official code. Although the authors explain their implementation choices to ensure a fair comparison, there remains some minor uncertainty regarding how this custom version compares to the original FLARE.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and challenging problem in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models: the conflict between low-dimensional, temporally smooth action trajectories and high-dimensional, spatially structured future visual observations when training a world model.

The proposed Dual-Stream Diffusion (DUST) architecture is elegant and well-designed, effectively balancing modality-specific processing (using separate streams and independent noise levels) with cross-modal interaction (using shared attention in MMDiT).

The decoupled noise scheduling during training and the asynchronous joint sampling at test time are theoretically grounded and highly practical, allowing for test-time scaling where the visual modality can be denoised with more steps than the action modality.

The empirical evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning two challenging simulation environments (RoboCasa and GR-1) as well as real-world experiments on a physical Franka robot. DUST consistently outperforms strong baselines like GR00T-N1.5 and FLARE.

The paper successfully demonstrates transfer learning by pre-training on action-free passive videos (BridgeV2), showing a substantial boost in downstream policy performance. This is a very promising direction for scaling up VLA models.
weaknesses: The paper lacks a detailed discussion or empirical measurement of the inference latency (FPS) overhead. Since the model generates both action and high-dimensional visual tokens, and particularly when using test-time scaling ($N_o = 16, 32, 64$), the computational cost at deployment could be significant compared to action-only VLAs. Providing concrete inference time comparisons would be highly beneficial.

While the paper compares DUST against FLARE (an implicit world model) and GR00T (action-only), it does not directly compare against a standard unified joint-diffusion world-model baseline (such as PAD or EnerVerse) using the same backbone. Such a baseline would further isolate the specific benefits of the dual-stream architecture over a single concatenated joint-diffusion model.

Because the world model operates in the latent space (predicting SIGLIP-2 embeddings), it is difficult to qualitatively assess what the world model is actually planning or predicting. Some qualitative visualizations of the predicted states (e.g., via a decoder or nearest-neighbor retrieval) would improve the interpretability of the learned dynamics.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a critical limitation in joint VLA and world-modeling frameworks: the statistical and dimensional mismatch between low-dimensional action trajectories and high-dimensional visual observation embeddings.
Proposes an elegant and technically sound dual-stream architecture (MMDiT with independent pathways but shared attention) coupled with a decoupled flow-matching training objective.
Introduces an innovative asynchronous joint sampling mechanism that allows test-time scaling by allocating more denoising steps to the visual modality than the action modality.

Provides a thorough empirical evaluation covering both simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1) and real-world experiments using a Franka Research 3 arm, consistently outperforming strong baselines like GR00T-N1.5 and FLARE.
Demonstrates excellent transfer learning performance from passive, action-free video datasets (BridgeV2), which is highly relevant for scaling up robotic policies.
Includes meticulous ablation studies that isolate the contributions of the architecture, decoupled noise schedules, loss weighting, and the depth of the MMDiT layers.
weaknesses: The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of inference latency and wall-clock times, especially when scaling up the number of vision denoising steps ($N_o > N_A$) at test time.

The approach is heavily dependent on the feature representation of a pre-trained VLM (SIGLIP-2 in Eagle-2), which may limit the applicability of the world model to domains not well represented by these pre-trained visual embeddings.
The performance gains on some simulated benchmarks under dense data regimes are somewhat incremental (e.g., around 1-2% average success rate improvement in some 1000-demo configurations).
Comparison against alternative non-diffusion world-model representations or planning-based baselines is limited.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and elegant dual-stream architecture (DUST) that resolves the fundamental trade-off between cross-modal integration and modality-specific fidelity in world-model augmented VLAs.

The decoupled joint training algorithm using independent noise scheduling is theoretically grounded and effectively forces the model to learn bidirectional causal relationships (forward and inverse dynamics).

The asynchronous joint sampling strategy is highly practical, enabling tunable test-time scaling where high-dimensional vision tokens can be denoised with more steps without slowing down or degrading low-dimensional action prediction.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation across diverse simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1, LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world Franka robot experiments demonstrates robust and consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines.
Strong transfer learning results are presented, successfully leveraging action-free videos for pretraining and heterogeneous datasets (human-robot mixtures) for joint-training.
weaknesses: The model's performance exhibits a strong dependency on high-quality visual inputs and predictions, which makes it particularly sensitive to visual occlusions and noisy camera feeds (as discussed in the real-world failure case analysis).

The baseline comparison for FLARE relies on a custom re-implementation because the original code is not publicly available. Although the authors put effort into making the comparison fair, it introduces some inherent baseline uncertainty.

The paper does not deeply explore the scaling behavior of the dual-stream transformer parameters (e.g., model capacity) and how that affects the quality of the learned world model relative to more heavy video-generation backbones (WAMs).

strengths: Well-motivated approach that resolves the modality gap in joint state-action modeling by combining separate token streams (via modified MMDiT) with cross-modal attention, decoupled noise schedules, and asynchronous sampling.

Extensive and highly thorough experimental evaluation across multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1, LIBERO, CALVIN) and physical real-world experiments on a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm, consistently demonstrating solid improvements over strong baselines like GR00T-N1.5 and FLARE.

Strong showing in transfer learning scenarios, successfully validating the framework's capability to utilize action-free videos for pretraining and heterogeneous robot-human data mixtures (e.g., EgoDex) for joint training.

Comprehensive ablation studies that clearly isolate the benefits of decoupled noise scheduling, MMDiT layers, latent representation types (SigLIP-2 vs. VAE), and the asynchronous test-time scaling strategy.
weaknesses: The core idea of decoupled noise scheduling is largely adapted from prior works (such as Diffusion Forcing and Diffuse Everything), somewhat bounding the conceptual novelty of the core training algorithm.

While the retargeting of human egocentric hand poses (EgoDex) to the Fourier action space is mentioned, details regarding how the coordinate alignment is managed during joint training across highly diverse embodiments could be more clearly explained.

The real-world failure case analysis highlights sensitivity to visual occlusions. Although the paper suggests future directions to resolve this, the current formulation lacks history (temporal context), which limits its robustness under momentary visual noise compared to sequence-based models.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework (DUST) that successfully addresses the modality-mismatch trade-off between low-dimensional action trajectories and high-dimensional visual states in world-model augmented VLAs.

Solid architectural and training innovations, including the use of an MMDiT backbone with separate stream pathways, decoupled modality-specific noise scheduling to learn bidirectional causal relationships, and an asynchronous joint sampling strategy during inference.

Exceptionally thorough and diverse empirical evaluation spanning multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1, LIBERO, CALVIN), real-world robot experiments on a Franka Research 3 arm, action-free video pretraining, and heterogeneous joint training.

Comprehensive ablation studies that isolate the contributions of different design choices, such as decoupled training, architecture, latent embedders (SigLIP-2 vs. DINOv2 vs. Flux VAE), and test-time step scaling.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, as several key components are adapted from existing works: MMDiT is from SD3/Flux, decoupled training is heavily inspired by Diffusion Forcing and Rojas et al., and semantic latent target prediction is similar to FLARE.
The world model is relatively short-horizon, only predicting a single future embedding corresponding to the end of the current action chunk rather than generating longer-horizon visual rollouts.

The inference latency benchmarks are conducted on a high-end RTX 5090 GPU; further validation on standard onboard robot hardware (e.g., Jetson Orin or mid-range GPUs) would better highlight its practical deployability.
